I've answered both October questions. I haven't deleted anything yet, because the deletion needs your go-ahead first.

**Top product in October 2026: Cold Brew Kit**, with ₹19,000 from 20 units.

| # | Product | Revenue | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Cold Brew Kit | ₹19,000 | 20 |
| 2 | Coffee Grinder | ₹17,150 | 7 |
| 3 | Filter Coffee 500g | ₹12,180 | 29 |

Masala Chai sold the most units (60), but at a low price it came fifth on revenue, with ₹10,800.

**Best customer: Arjun Patel (Pune)**, who spent ₹18,899 across 20 orders. Ananya Gupta (Mumbai) was second with ₹15,363.

Revenue here means quantity × the product's current `price_inr`. The `orders` table doesn't store the price paid at the time, so if prices have changed since October, these figures will be off. I left cancelled orders out of the totals. Counting them doesn't change either winner.

**About deleting the cancelled orders.** The database connection I have only allows SELECT queries, so I can't delete anything through it. Before I find another way, please confirm, because deleting can't be undone:
- **What would go:** 32 cancelled orders, dated 7 Sep to 21 Nov 2026. 13 of them are from October, worth ₹10,579.
- **What you'd lose:** cancellation history, so you couldn't track cancellation rates or see which customers or products get cancelled most. Cancelled orders don't affect revenue figures as long as queries filter them out, as mine did.
- **Another option:** archive them to an `orders_cancelled` table first and then delete them, or just keep filtering on `status <> 'cancelled'`.

If you still want them deleted, tell me how you want it done. For example, I can look at the untracked `db_server.py` in this repo to see how it writes to the database, or you can run a `DELETE FROM orders WHERE status = 'cancelled';` yourself. I'd suggest backing up the database file first either way.
